brief_context: Refers to both sides of the ocean regarding consumer trends.
article_title: Consumerism — is it still about consumers?
brief_extract: It is interesting to compare present trends in the USA with those in this country. On both sides of the Atlantic we are seeing the emergence of so-called ‘consumer professionals’ who are creating a new calling based upon the need for expertise in representing the whole range of consumer needs, demands and aspirations. There are, however, differences between the British and the American approaches to consumer pro-fessionalism, and it is worth examining these in some depth because they are divergent, and that divergence is significant because it could create in Britain a stultifying and counter-productive trend.

brief_context: Refers to the consumer movement system within the United Kingdom.
brief_extract: Think of the time that can be saved and the problems which can be averted by consumer thinking being geared into basic planning. Under the present British system we see the consumer movement drifting into an ever deepening perpetuation of the 'them and us' situation. Instead of joint constructive effort and partnership in planning, the British movement sticks to a pattern of separate development; with those making decisions on the one hand locked in continuing wrangles with those who, on the other, are dissatisfied with these decisions.

brief_context: Refers to trends in consumer advocacy within the United States.
brief_extract: The EAW believes in co-operation and in helping industry and commerce to realise that consumerism is not 'the enemy' but a movement with much to offer in terms of constructive thinking which can lead to better business and, yes, to higher profits. The American trend, with 'consumer advocates' actually on the pay-roll of companies, may sound unrealistic but nevertheless it works. Such consumer professionals are dedicated to genuine consumer representation of the highest standard, and their target is the company.

brief_context: Discussed in relation to the future of consumerism.
brief_extract: Surely, without recourse to interviewing and opinion-testing facilities it is almost impossible for such individuals do more than express personal attitudes. Perhaps we should aspire to more imaginative consumerism in Britain over the approaching decade. Consumers can help to get a better deal for themselves not by 'leaving it all to the experts' but by participating in consumer affairs and by taking advantage of all the facilities which exist to provide them with education and information.

Have you ever bought a typewriter, sewing machine, TV set or other product described by the manufacturer as 'portable' and found it far too heavy to carry any distance with comfort? According to a survey carried out by the United States National Bureau of Standards, the answer to the question 'when is a portable object really portable?' is 'when it weighs no more than 10.7 kg'. The result is based on a series of tests involving a group of people aged between 16 and 65, and that weight is considered to be the absolute limit in order to satisfy 90% of consumers.

brief_context: Mentioned as a region where electric blankets are popular.
article_title: Dreamland, Alarmline, Monogram feature by Susi Luss
brief_extract: Some of you may be pre-heating underblanket fans while others swear by all-night overblankets — but in either case you need no convincing on the relative merits and demerits of electric blankets. Dreamland-Monogram, who have been in the business for over 30 years now, are in the happy position of producing 17,000 over- and under-blankets a week and of knowing that well over half the homes in Britain are electric blanket users, making them about as popular as the motor car. I was interested in finding out more about Monogram's Continuous Sensor protection system, which they incorporate into all their overblankets.

brief_context: Site of the 10-acre electric blanket production factory.
article_title: Dreamland, Alarmline, Monogram feature by Susi Luss
brief_extract: Norah Riddington, EAW Services Administrator, whose work on various BSI safety committees includes electric blankets, was equally intrigued by the manufacture and servicing aspects. On a scorching day last summer (hardly conducive to concentrating on cuddly blankets however) we were shown the 10 acres of electric blanket production at Hythe. Almost every component is manufactured in their own works, even the underblanket material, a mixture of viscose and rayon with a cotton warp.

brief_context: Refers to UK electric blanket usage and servicing statistics.
brief_extract: As electrical women, EAW members know that their electric blankets should be returned for servicing at least every two to three years but there is no harm in repeating such an important safety reminder. Of the 10 to 12 million electric blankets in use in this country approximately 100,000 are serviced each year. Apart from their own models, Dreamland-Monogram are occasionally sent blankets made by manufacturers who went out of business years ago and not necessarily manufactured to current standards.

article_title: Pigeon Post: Letter from Miriam R. Wood regarding local advertising
brief_extract:
Dear Editor,
It Pays to Advertise
During the year we have obtained sixteen new members and expect another one or two next month. We attribute this to the window display we put on in a local Building Society on The Grove, to an advertisement in our local weekly newspaper, recruiting literature placed in the library and the fact that we sent a copy of our programme to the Women's Page Editor of our County evening paper and get regular mentions in that paper. This year we celebrate our 21st Birthday and aim to bring our new membership for the year to 21.
